title: Kerberoasting

attack.summary: Any authenticated domain user can request a Kerberos service ticket (TGS) for an account that has a Service Principal Name. The ticket is encrypted with the service account's password hash, which the attacker extracts and cracks offline — no elevated access is needed to request it.
attack.commandNote: Illustrative / lab-only. Shown to explain the artifact, not for use against systems you don't own.

keyFields.whyItMatters: Modern AD uses AES (0x12/0x11); an RC4 TGS request is the anomaly roasting tools force so the hash is crackable.
Identifies which service account was targeted.

detection.rule:
title: Kerberoasting Activity Detection
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 4769
    TicketEncryptionType: '0x17'
  filter:
    ServiceName: 'krbtgt'
  condition: selection and not filter
level: high

annotations.explain: Only look at Kerberos service-ticket (TGS) requests.
RC4 — the weak cipher a roasting tool forces so the extracted hash is crackable offline. This is the core signal.
Exclude the krbtgt account, whose 4769s are normal, to cut noise.

falsePositives: Legacy applications or systems that legitimately still negotiate RC4.
Older service accounts not yet migrated to AES.

mitigation.summary: Remove the crackable material and the weak cipher.
controls: Enforce AES-only Kerberos; disable RC4 where possible.
Use long (25+ char) or group-managed service-account passwords (gMSA).
Alert on RC4 TGS requests; investigate bulk SPN enumeration.
